facts.fact: Small tanks change temperature and water chemistry faster than large ones, so they are less stable and need more frequent testing.
Filtration is critical in a nano tank because its water quality can shift quickly.
Put the tank on a level surface that can hold its full weight, near a power outlet, away from direct sunlight, windows, doors, vents and air conditioners.
Rinse the tank, check it for cracks, and partly fill it to test for leaks.
Rinse non-bioactive gravel before adding it, then add decor and arrange the layout.
Substrate of sand, gravel or crushed stone can be 2 cm to 7 cm deep, with an optional 2 cm to 3 cm nutrient soil layer underneath.
Gravel of about 3 mm is popular for medium-sized tanks.
Place rocks and driftwood before planting, positioning rocks to give small fish shelter.
Fit filter, heater, thermometer and light per the maker's instructions, and do not switch anything on until the tank is full.
Treat tap water with a conditioner to neutralize chlorine or chloramine.
Tap water can be dechlorinated by letting it stand for 24 hours or with a commercial dechlorinator.
Run all equipment for 24 to 48 hours to settle and to confirm it works before maturing the filter.
Loop power cords downward before the outlet (drip loop) so water cannot run into sockets.
Cycle the tank before adding fish, testing daily for ammonia, nitrite and nitrate.
Natural cycling usually takes four to six weeks, or a few days with beneficial bacteria products.
In a fishless cycle, fish food or another ammonia source is added to the empty tank to grow beneficial bacteria.
Used filter media from a trusted, established tank can speed cycling to a matter of weeks.
The filter is mature when ammonia and nitrite stay at zero while nitrate rises.
Ammonia and nitrite should be 0 mg/L in a freshwater tank.
Add fish soon after cycling ends, since the bacteria need a food source.
Acclimatise fish by floating the sealed bag about 10 minutes, then slowly adding tank water over up to 20 minutes; drip acclimation over hours suits sensitive species.
Plants start to establish after about 2 weeks and grow fast after about 1 month.
Test kits for ammonia, nitrite, nitrate and pH are needed; a hardness kit is also useful.
Choose LED lights for nano tanks and avoid heat-producing lights; kit lights may be too weak for planted tanks.
Plants suggested for nano tanks include Cryptocoryne wendtii, C. pygmaea, Echinodorus tenellus, Marsilea crenata and Anubias barteri var. nana.
Nano tank fish suggested include Boraras brigittae, Danio margaritatus, Poecilia wingei, Betta splendens and Corydoras pygmaeus, plus cherry shrimp Neocaridina davidi.
Java fern's rhizome should not be buried in the substrate; tie or glue it to rock or wood.
Cryptocoryne wendtii feeds mainly through its roots; in inert substrate add root tabs about every three months, and it needs no CO2.
Cryptocoryne leaves may melt after planting; leave the plant in place and it usually recovers.
Change water at least weekly in a nano tank, preferably more often.
Change up to 25% of the water weekly and test water at least once a week.
Match new water to tank temperature during water changes to avoid shocking fish.
Feed only what fish eat in 60 seconds.
In a small planted tank, split the weekly fertilizer dose into seven daily doses to limit algae.
Vacuum the top layer of substrate to remove organic waste, even in planted tanks.
Add fish slowly; each addition needs a mini-cycle for the filter to catch up.
Adding fish too early or too many at once causes new tank syndrome, with ammonia or nitrite poisoning that can kill fish.
Rinsing filter media under the tap kills beneficial bacteria; rinse it in removed tank water.
Filter media from an untrusted source can bring pests and pathogens.
Fish-in cycling stresses fish and risks ammonia spikes.
Choosing a tank too small for the adult size of the fish is a common mistake.
Mixing shrimp colour morphs leads to crossbreeding.
Never siphon aquarium water by mouth.
During a power cut, do not feed or change water in the first 1-2 hours.
In outages over 8 hours, run an air stone or sponge filter for 1 hour every 8 hours, or every 4 hours if fish gasp or the tank is heavily stocked.
A USB air pump can run from a power bank during outages.
In hot weather, a fan blowing across the surface cools water by evaporation; avoid floating frozen bottles because fast temperature change stresses fish.
After power returns, wait 24 hours before feeding and change water if ammonia or nitrite is above 0 ppm.
Keep the tank where water changes and glass and substrate cleaning are easy.
